[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding CAP and PACELC Theorems in System Design"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When designing distributed data stores, understanding the theoretical limits of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance is paramount. This tutorial covers the foundational CAP theorem and its modern evolution, the PACELC theorem."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The CAP Theorem Fundamentals"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Formulated by Eric Brewer, the CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of the following three guarantees:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a non-error response, without the guarantee that it contains the most recent write."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Why Partition Tolerance is Non-Negotiable"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"In real-world network architectures, network partitions (P) are inevitable due to hardware failures, cable cuts, or routing issues. Therefore, distributed systems must choose between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP) during a partition."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"The Limitation of CAP"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"While CAP is useful, it only describes system behavior during a network partition. It says nothing about the system's behavior during normal operations (when there is no partition), which is when databases spend 99% of their time. This limitation led to the creation of the PACELC theorem."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"The PACELC Theorem"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Proposed by Daniel Abadi, the PACELC theorem extends CAP by evaluating system trade-offs in two distinct states: when there is a partition, and else (during normal operations)."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If there is a Partition (P), how does the system choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C)?"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Else (E), when the system is running normally without partitions, how does the system choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C)?"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"PACELC Classifications"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Databases can be categorized based on their PACELC profile:"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PC/EC (e.g., Google Spanner, HBase, ZooKeeper): Chooses consistency over availability during partitions, and consistency over latency during normal operations."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PA/EL (e.g., DynamoDB, Cassandra): Chooses availability over consistency during partitions, and low latency over consistency during normal operations."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PA/EC (e.g., MongoDB default configuration): Chooses availability during partitions, but favors consistency (by routing reads to primary nodes) during normal operations."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Architecture Example"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider a configuration snippet for a distributed system establishing quorum reads and writes:"},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"const dbConfig = {
  clusterName: "user_service_cluster",
  partitionHandling: "availability",
  normalOperation: "latency",
  writeQuorum: 2,
  readQuorum: 1
};"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"By setting readQuorum to 1 and writeQuorum to 2 in a PA/EL system, you trade consistency for faster response times during normal operations, accepting eventual consistency."}]
